extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (or beginning graduate) students studying real analysis / metric-space based calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material developing limits, continuity, sequences/series (including rearrangements and Cauchy products), compactness/connectedness, uniform continuity, and differentiation (definitions, rules, and mean value theorems) in metric spaces and on real intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of a function (metric-space epsilon–delta definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: lim_{x→x0} f(x) = y0 if for any ε>0 there exists δ>0 so that any x∈U with 0 < d_X(x,x0) < δ implies d_Y(f(x),y0) < ε. If no such y0 exists the limit doesn't exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require x0∈U' (a limit point) so there are points x with 0<d_X(x,x0)<δ. Remarks include: (1) the usual ℝ absolute-value specialization; (2) limit is a local property (depends only on values of f in any small neighborhood of x0); (3) f(x0) need not be defined for the limit to exist; (4) nonexistence can be expressed via existence of ε0>0 so that for any δ>0 there exists x with 0<d_X(x,x0)<δ but d_Y(f(x),y0)≥ε0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence characterization of limits of functions (Proposition 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: lim_{x→x0} f(x) = y0 iff for every sequence {x_n} in U\{x0} that converges to x0 we have f(x_n)→y0. Conversely, nonexistence can be witnessed by some sequence converging to x0 with f(x_n) not converging to y0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a method to prove existence/nonexistence of limits by considering sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of limits (Proposition 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→x0} f(x) exists then it is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two standard proofs: (1) epsilon–delta triangle inequality argument; (2) via sequence characterization and uniqueness of sequence limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra of limits for functions (Proposition 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→x0} f(x)=A and lim_{x→x0} g(x)=B (real-valued), then (f±g)→A±B, (f·g)→A·B, (f/g)→A/B provided B≠0, and (c·f)→cA for c∈ℝ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs may use sequence characterization: apply algebraic limit properties for sequences. Exercises left to reader for some parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity at a point (Definition 2.1) including isolated point case
rubrics_metrics.description: f:U→Y is continuous at x0∈U if either (1) x0 is isolated in U, or (2) x0∈U∩U' and lim_{x→x0} f(x) = f(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity can be rephrased by an ε–δ condition: for any ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that d_X(x,x0)<δ and x∈U implies d_Y(f(x),f(x0))<ε. Example classes: polynomials, rationals on their domain, exp, sin, cos, x^α (α>0) are continuous on natural domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent open/closed preimage characterization of continuity (Proposition 2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: f is continuous on X iff the preimage f^{-1}(V) of every open subset V⊂Y is open in X. Equivalently, iff preimage of every closed V⊂Y is closed in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses ε–δ definition; conversely use openness of preimages of ε-balls to recover continuity. For general topological spaces this is the definition of continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra of continuous functions (Proposition 2.3 / Corollary 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are continuous at x0 then f±g, f·g, f/g (if g(x0)≠0), and c·f (c∈ℝ) are continuous at x0. Composition of continuous functions is continuous. Polynomials, exponentials, sine/cosine, x^α (α>0) are continuous on their natural domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use limit algebra or sequence characterization. Composition continuity uses image of δ-ball inside ε-ball argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous image of a compact set is compact (Theorem 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:X→Y is continuous and K⊂X is compact, then f(K) is compact in Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via open-cover preimage argument using continuity (or via sequences: sequentially compact → image sequentially compact). Corollary: f(K) is closed and bounded in ℝ; hence continuous real-valued functions on compact sets attain max and min (Theorem 3.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous bijection inverse continuity under compact domain (Theorem 3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:X→Y is a continuous bijection and X is compact, then f^{-1}:f(X)→X is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples show inverse of continuous bijection need not be continuous without compactness. Proofs: (1) show f is an open map using compactness, or (2) sequence argument using sequential compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform continuity (Definition 3.10) and equivalence on compact domains (Theorem 3.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: f:X→Y is uniformly continuous if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that any x1,x2∈X with d_X(x1,x2)<δ implies d_Y(f(x1),f(x2))<ε. On a compact domain, continuity ⇔ uniform continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform continuity implies pointwise continuity. Proof that continuity on compact implies uniform uses open cover of X by balls of radii δ(x)/2 and finite subcover to obtain a uniform δ. A sequence-based proof by contradiction is also provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectedness and continuity (Theorem 4.4 & IVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is connected and f:X→Y is continuous then f(X) is connected. For f continuous on a closed interval [a,b], the Intermediate Value Theorem: if f(a)<f(b) then for any y0 with f(a)<y0<f(b) there exists x0∈(a,b) with f(x0)=y0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connectedness of [a,b] (and path-connectedness) is used. IVT is a direct corollary of continuous images preserving connectedness; remark emphasizes need for closed interval hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path-connectedness (Definition 4.6) and relation to connectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: A space X is path-connected if any two points x0,x1∈X can be joined by a continuous map f:[0,1]→X with f(0)=x0,f(1)=x1. Every path-connected space is connected; in ℝ these notions coincide for subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exercise: [0,1] is path-connected and thus connected; topologist's sine curve shows connected does not imply path-connected in ℝ^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonic functions: existence of one-sided limits (Theorem 5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:(a,b)→ℝ is increasing then for any x0∈(a,b) the one-sided limits f(x0−) := lim_{x→x0−} f(x) and f(x0+) := lim_{x→x0+} f(x) exist, with sup_{a<t<x0} f(t)=f(x0−) ≤ f(x0) ≤ f(x0+) = inf_{x0<t<b} f(t). Moreover for a<x<y<b, f(x+) ≤ f(y−).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses monotonicity to show bounded monotone sets have l.u.b./g.l.b. Corollary: monotonic functions have no second-kind discontinuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of discontinuities for monotone functions (Theorem 5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:(a,b)→ℝ is monotonic then the set of discontinuity points is at most countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: at each discontinuity x there is a jump f(x−)<f(x+); choose a rational r_x between the jump endpoints to inject discontinuities into ℚ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of series (Proposition 2.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ a_n = A and Σ b_n = B (convergent), then Σ(a_n + b_n) = A + B, and for any c∈ℝ, Σ(c·a_n) = cA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard properties of series; proofs follow from partial sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy product (definition and caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given formal series Σ a_n and Σ b_n, define c_n := Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n−k}; the series Σ c_n is the Cauchy product (formal product). However Σ a_n · Σ b_n ≠ A·B in general; the Cauchy product may fail to converge even if both series converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: conditionally convergent alternating series whose Cauchy product produces terms c_n that do not tend to 0, hence Σ c_n diverges. Remark: c_n is not in general equal to (Σ_{k=0}^n a_k)(Σ_{k=0}^n b_k) etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mertens' theorem on Cauchy product (Theorem 2.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ a_n = A and Σ b_n = B and Σ a_n converges absolutely, then the Cauchy product Σ c_n (with c_n=Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n−k}) converges and Σ c_n = AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given via partial sums manipulation and estimation using absolute convergence of Σ|a_k| and convergence of partial sums of b_n; uses ε–N style splitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abel's result on Cauchy product (Theorem 2.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ a_n = A, Σ b_n = B and the Cauchy product Σ c_n converges to C (where c_n=Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n−k}), then C = AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Abel's result; will be proved later using continuity of power series. It asserts that whenever the Cauchy product converges, its sum equals the product of sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement of series and Riemann's theorem (Theorem 2.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rearrangement of Σ x_n uses a bijection r:ℤ+→ℤ+ and the series Σ x_{r(n)}. If Σ x_n converges but not absolutely, then for any a≤b (including ±∞) there exists a rearrangement whose partial sums S'_n satisfy liminf S'_n = a and limsup S'_n = b. In particular, for any real a there exists a rearrangement summing to a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: alternating harmonic series rearranged to give a different sum. Proof reference to Rudin Theorem 3.54.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangements of absolutely convergent series preserve sum (Theorem 2.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ x_n is absolutely convergent then every rearrangement converges absolutely to the same limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses tail control: given ε>0 pick N so tails have small absolute sum, then arrange indices to show any sufficiently large partial sum of rearrangement differs by <ε. Details left to reader for equality of limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability definition and implication (Definition 1.1 & Proposition 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: f:[a,b]→ℝ is differentiable at x0 if the limit φ_{x0}(t) = (f(t)-f(x0))/(t-x0) (t→x0) exists; denote f'(x0) as this limit. If f is differentiable at x0 then f is continuous at x0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: differentiability implies continuity by expressing difference as quotient times |x−x0| and taking limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for derivatives: sum, product, quotient (Theorem 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are differentiable at x0, then (f±g)'(x0)=f'(x0)±g'(x0); (f·g)'(x0)=f'(x0)g(x0)+f(x0)g'(x0); (f/g)'(x0)=(f'(x0)g(x0)-f(x0)g'(x0))/g(x0)^2 when g(x0)≠0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use algebraic rearrangement of difference quotients and previous continuity result; example proofs left for some parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain rule (Theorem 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable at x0 and g is differentiable at f(x0) then h=g∘f is differentiable at x0 and h'(x0)=g'(f(x0))·f'(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses o(|x−x0|) notation: write local linear approximations g(y)-g(f(x0))=(g'(f(x0))+o(|y−f(x0)|))(y-f(x0)) and f(x)-f(x0)=f'(x0)(x−x0)+o(|x−x0|), multiply and take limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical points and local extrema (Theorem 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has a local maximum or minimum at x0∈(a,b) and is differentiable at x0, then x0 is a critical point: f'(x0)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: sign of difference quotient on either side gives one-sided derivatives ≥0 and ≤0 respectively; equality of one-sided derivatives yields zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolle's theorem (Theorem 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) and f(a)=f(b), then there exists x0∈(a,b) with f'(x0)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply extreme value theorem to find interior max/min then use critical point theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean Value Theorem (Theorem 2.5) and Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem (Theorem 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) then ∃x0∈(a,b) with f(b)-f(a)=f'(x0)(b-a). Cauchy's version: if f,g continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) then ∃x0 s.t. (f(b)-f(a))g'(x0)=(g(b)-g(a))f'(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mean value theorem follows from Rolle by applying to f(x) minus the secant-line; Cauchy’s theorem uses an auxiliary linear combination h(x)=(f(b)-f(a))g(x)-(g(b)-g(a))f(x) and Rolle's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative sign implies monotonicity (Theorem 2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable on (a,b) then f'≥0 implies f is increasing; f'≤0 implies decreasing; f'=0 implies constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply mean value theorem on subintervals: difference equals derivative at some interior point times interval length.
